data.scenario_text: The function <me>H(t)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)\right]+42</me> models a rider's height, in feet, above the ground on a Ferris wheel, where <m>t</m> is the number of minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 3 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=42, so the rider averages \boxed{42\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=42+16=58\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=42-16=26\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 58\text{ ft} 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 26\text{ ft} 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[26\text{ ft},\ 58\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 11 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 8 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=30, so the rider averages \boxed{30\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=30+22=52\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=30-22=8\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 52\text{ ft} 6 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 8\text{ ft} 12 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 52\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)=0 \implies t-3=0 \implies t=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 3 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 3 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 6 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 12 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=8 (8 minutes after the ride starts):

H(8)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(8-3)\right]+30=22\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+30=52\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a height of about \boxed{52.0\text{ ft}} 8 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 7 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=41, so the rider averages \boxed{41\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=41+16=57\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=41-16=25\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 57\text{ ft} 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 25\text{ ft} 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[25\text{ ft},\ 57\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=7 (7 minutes after the ride starts):

H(7)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-2)\right]+41=16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+41=57\text{ ft}

data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 6 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=32, so the rider averages \boxed{32\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=32+22=54\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=32-22=10\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 54\text{ ft} 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 10\text{ ft} 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 54\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=6 (6 minutes after the ride starts):

H(6)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-2)\right]+32=22\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+32=11 \, \sqrt{3} + 32 \approx 51.1\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a height of about \boxed{51.1\text{ ft}} 6 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 10 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=31, so the rider averages \boxed{31\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=31+24=55\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=31-24=7\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 55\text{ ft} 6 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 7\text{ ft} 12 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 55\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)=0 \implies t-3=0 \implies t=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 3 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 3 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 6 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 12 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=10 (10 minutes after the ride starts):

H(10)=24\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-3)\right]+31=24\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+31=7\text{ ft}

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 10 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=32, so the rider averages \boxed{32\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=32+16=48\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=32-16=16\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 48\text{ ft} 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 16\text{ ft} 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[16\text{ ft},\ 48\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=10 (10 minutes after the ride starts):

H(10)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+32=16\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+32=-8 \, \sqrt{3} + 32 \approx 18.1\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a height of about \boxed{18.1\text{ ft}} 10 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height 5 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=36, so the rider averages \boxed{36\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=36+20=56\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=36-20=16\text{ ft}

the rider reaches a maximum of 56\text{ ft} 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 16\text{ ft} 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[16\text{ ft},\ 56\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

The phase shift is \boxed{1} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 1 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising 1 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top 4 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest 10 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=5 (5 minutes after the ride starts):

H(5)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-1)\right]+36=20\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+36=10 \, \sqrt{3} + 36 \approx 53.3\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a height of about \boxed{53.3\text{ ft}} 5 minutes after the ride starts.
